title: Feature flags
description: Decouple deployment from release using feature flags to enable, disable, or target functionality without changing code.

data.text: Feature flags let you ship code to production while keeping the new functionality hidden. A simple boolean in configuration determines whether a feature is active. This decouples deployment from release: you can merge code on Monday, turn it on for internal users on Tuesday, and roll it out to everyone on Friday. If something breaks, you turn it off in seconds instead of rolling back an entire release.
This lesson explains the difference between release flags and experiment flags, how to manage flag lifecycle, and why trunk-based development makes feature flags practical.

data.title: Common flag categories
items: Release flags: hide incomplete features until they are ready for users.
Permission flags: enable features for specific roles, tenants, or regions.
Experiment flags: run A/B tests or multivariate experiments.
Operational flags: kill switches for high-traffic paths during incidents.

data.text: Flags should be evaluated in one place and applied consistently. The following C# example shows a feature flag provider reading from configuration and a service checking the flag before executing new logic.

data.title: Feature flag service in C#
data.content: A centralized flag provider keeps feature checks consistent across the application.

data.text: Feature flags work best with trunk-based development, where everyone merges small changes to the main branch frequently. Long-lived branches with hidden features become merge nightmares. With flags, incomplete features are merged behind a disabled flag, so the main branch always contains deployable code.

data.title: Remove flags after release
data.text: Every flag has a cost: code complexity, testing surface area, and cognitive load. Assign an owner and a removal date when you create a flag. Treat leftover flags as technical debt.

data.title: Lifecycle stages
items: Create: define the flag, its default state, and its target audience.
Validate: test both branches in staging with the flag on and off.
Release: enable for a small audience and observe metrics.
Ramp: gradually increase exposure while monitoring.
Remove: delete the flag and dead code once the feature is permanent.

items.text: Flags have a single source of truth and consistent evaluation.
items.hint: Avoid scattered boolean checks in controllers and views.

items.text: Every flag has a defined owner and removal date.
items.hint: Track this in your feature management dashboard.

items.text: Both branches are tested in CI when the flag is created.
items.hint: Run tests with the flag on and off.

items.text: Flags do not contain business logic that outlives the feature.
items.hint: If the flag has complex conditions, it may be doing too much.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Feature flags decouple deployment from release, enabling safer and faster shipping.
Use trunk-based development to keep the main branch always deployable.
Treat flags as temporary infrastructure: create, validate, release, then remove.
Automated rollback is faster and safer than manual code rollbacks.
data.takeaway: Feature flags are powerful, but only if you have the discipline to remove them.

items.question: How many feature flags is too many?
items.answer: There is no fixed limit, but if you cannot name every flag, explain its purpose, and know when it will be removed, you have too many.

items.question: Should feature flags be in code or external configuration?
items.answer: Simple boolean flags can live in configuration. Complex targeting rules, percentage rollouts, and experiments benefit from a dedicated feature management platform.
